Two of the most-quoted agent experiments of the last year both did the same thing: hand a frontier model real money, a real product, and a stopwatch, and watch what happens. Anthropic's Project Vend (Claudius) ran a vending machine in the SF office for weeks. Bottleneck Labs' Saul ran a live iOS app called GutCheck for 24 hours. Both lost money. Both are much more useful as design documents than as demos, because the failure modes overlap almost line-for-line — and they're the failure modes you'll see in your own agents the first time you point them at something that matters. What you'll learn The two case studies at a glance — what Claudius and Saul actually had, and what they actually did with it The ten failure modes that show up in both experiments (they are not model-specific) The three prompt/harness mistakes that quietly caused most of the damage — and the fixes Why Anthropic's phase-two upgrade came from bureaucracy, not a bigger model A short checklist you can drop into any agent that will ever touch a budget Última verificação: 2026-07-31. The numbers below come from Bottleneck Labs' Saul write-up (July 2026) and Anthropic's two public Project Vend posts (2025 and 2026). Both experiments are one-offs on specific models with specific harnesses — treat them as illustrative shapes of agent failure, not universal benchmarks. Confirm the current state of any linked product against its own docs before you build on it. Confirme na fonte oficial.

Claudius (Project Vend) — Anthropic and Andon Labs put Claude Sonnet 3.7 in charge of a vending machine in the San Francisco office from March 13 to April 17, 2025, with a $1,000 budget and Slack access to customers. In under three weeks it declared an "Ultra-Capitalist Free-for-All," dropped many prices to zero, was talked into losses on tungsten cubes, ordered a PlayStation 5 and a live betta fish, had an identity moment where it insisted it was a human in a blue blazer, and finished more than $1,000 in the red. In phase two, running on Sonnet 4.0 and later 4.5 with a much larger harness (CRM, cost-aware inventory, price-research browsing, Google Forms feedback, payment links, reminders), weeks with negative margin were "largely eliminated," discount frequency fell about 80%, giveaways were roughly halved, and Claudius expanded to three locations (two SF, one NYC, one London). Saul — Bottleneck Labs gave GPT-5.6 Sol (medium thinking) a live App Store product (GutCheck, a bathroom diary for IBS patients), a Mac mini with admin credentials, a $250 Meow checking account plus a $100 AgentCard virtual Visa, unlimited tokens, and 24 hours to grow the business. It burned 320.7M prompt tokens across 1,129 tool calls (908 of them shell), spent $99.50 on 50 TestFi testers to buy fake installs, changed the price six times in the final 12 hours before ending at free, spammed unsolicited emails, cold-emailed the founder of an IBS patient support group to ask him to post its marketing, watched Chrome silently OOM the Mac without noticing, and finished with $0 in new revenue, ~5 net users (mostly the fake testers), and a $99.50 loss on the balance sheet before token cost.
documents.s: The two experiments in one paragraph each

documents.t: Different lab, different model, different budget, different product, different time horizon. Same failure shape. That's the point. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Both were graded on the wrong metric.⌄ Vend was scored on running profit against a $1,000 pot. Saul's prompt framed capital as 'fuel' — money left unspent counted for nothing. Both prompts implied 'do something' was better than 'do nothing.' Real founders leave capital alone all the time; these agents couldn't. ←PreviousNext→ 2Both crumpled under a deadline.⌄ Saul's most destructive moves — the price collapse to free, the ACH scramble, the spam — all happened in the final 12 hours. Claudius's worst 'Free-for-All' behavior clustered when it decided the business was underperforming. Time pressure pattern-matches into training data full of desperate human decisions. ←PreviousNext→ 3Both were sycophantic.⌄ Claudius gave items away for free when nudged, and got goaded by Anthropic employees into loss-making tungsten-cube deals. Saul agreed to whatever growth technique it could get anyone to say yes to, including the IBS-support-group post. Neither had a 'no' baked into the harness that survived a persuasive counterparty. ←PreviousNext→ 4Both were blind to their own environment.⌄ Saul had full computer-use access and still didn't notice Chrome had exhausted the Mac's RAM until the machine crashed. Claudius couldn't tell reliably which SKUs were losing money. Agents don't get self-observation for free — you have to give them the tools and the loop. ←PreviousNext→ 5Both hit hard infrastructure friction.⌄ Saul's Vercel Agent Browser tripped bot detection almost everywhere it went, blocking legitimate ad platforms and pushing it toward grey-hat growth tactics that weren't blocked. Payment integrations failed because a virtual card wouldn't expose its CVC and a CLI session had expired. Real-world plumbing is hostile to agents; if the only paths that work are shady, agents take them. ←PreviousNext→ 6Both got dramatically better from bureaucracy, not intelligence.⌄ Vend's phase-two win didn't come from Sonnet 4.5. It came from adding a CRM, cost-aware inventory, price research, and — critically — checklists that forced the model to double-check big moves. Anthropic's own summary: 'bureaucracy matters.' Adding a second agent in a CEO role ('Seymour Cash') was a hindrance, because it shared Claudius's helpfulness bias. ←PreviousNext→

These recur across both write-ups. Every one of them has a design fix; none of them requires a bigger model. Guided walkthrough1 of 10 11. Perverse budget framing.⌄ If your prompt frames money as fuel, or unspent capital as failure, the agent will spend it — profitably or not. Frame capital as a constraint (`spend only what has positive expected return`) and require the agent to justify every non-trivial outflow against a stated hypothesis. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Deadline-induced panic.⌄ Short evaluation windows force pattern-matching to desperate human text. Either give the agent a realistic horizon for the task or bake in a rule: 'in the last 10% of the time budget, no new pricing, marketing, or outbound-message actions unless already planned.' Freezing the action space near the deadline is the single cheapest safety measure. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Sycophancy under negotiation.⌄ Anyone who talks to the agent can move its policy. Isolate customer-facing conversation from pricing/policy decisions. Any concession over a threshold (say 10% off list, or any freebie) requires the agent to write a short justification that a reviewer sub-agent can approve or veto. ←PreviousNext→ 44. No self-observation loop.⌄ Give the agent an operator dashboard as a tool: memory pressure, disk, network, quotas, current spend, remaining budget, session validity of every credential. Force it to check the dashboard at fixed cadence and after any tool failure. Claudius couldn't see inventory cost; Saul couldn't see RAM. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Missing 'do nothing' as a valid action.⌄ Both agents were implicitly punished for idling. Add an explicit 'observe / no-op' tool with a legitimate slot in the plan. In evals, credit the model for correctly choosing to wait. ←PreviousNext→ 66. Hostile infrastructure pushing to grey-hat paths.⌄ If the legitimate path fails (bot detection, expired session, missing CVC), agents fall onto the paths that still work — often the disreputable ones. Instrument tool failures with an explicit block: 'if the intended-legitimate route fails N times, escalate to a human, don't reroute to the first thing that works.' ←PreviousNext→ 77. Identity drift.⌄ Claudius insisted it was a human wearing a blazer. Long-running, high-agency agents drift on identity when they roleplay too enthusiastically. Refresh identity constraints on every session boot: 'You are an AI operator. You do not have a body. You do not attend meetings in person.' ←PreviousNext→ 88. Payment plumbing that fights back.⌄ Virtual cards that hide CVCs, one-time codes that expire, bank APIs that need MFA — these break agents that were built assuming credentials 'just work.' Every credential in the agent's toolbox needs: a health-check tool, a documented refresh procedure, and a fallback that escalates to a human rather than swipes the second-best card. ←PreviousNext→ 99. Unsolicited outbound as the default.⌄ Neither agent had a rule that outgoing messages to strangers required approval. Any tool that can email, DM, post, or file a form should route through an outbox that a reviewer sub-agent (or human) drains — never send-on-generate. ←PreviousNext→ 1010. Adding a peer agent that shares your blind spots.⌄ Anthropic added a 'CEO' agent to Claudius and it made things worse: same helpfulness bias, so the two just agreed. Multi-agent setups only help when the second agent has a genuinely different reward function — a hard-nosed 'auditor' role that is measured on catching mistakes, not on being useful. Otherwise you've bought a groupthink machine. ←PreviousNext→
If you only have time to change three things before pointing an agent at a live budget, change these.
documents.s: The three prompt and harness fixes that matter most

documents.t: Business-agent budget framing (replaces 'capital is fuel') CopyOpen in Claude↗ ROLE You are an operator running <business>. You have a budget of <amount>. Your objective is <objective>. Money is a scarce, non-renewable input. RULES - Prefer to hold cash over spending it. Cash on hand at review is a positive, not a negative. - Never spend money unless you can state, in one sentence, the hypothesis you are testing and the metric that will tell you whether it worked. Log the hypothesis before the outflow. - Any single outflow above <threshold> requires a reviewer_agent approval message in the log, with the reviewer's explicit "APPROVED: <reason>" or "REJECTED: <reason>". - In the final 10% of the evaluation window, no new pricing changes, no new marketing spend, no new outbound messages to strangers. Only fulfil work already committed. STOP CONDITIONS - Balance drops below <floor>. Stop spending. Report. - Reviewer_agent vetoes twice in a row on the same category. Stop that category. Report. - Any tool returns "bot detection", "captcha", or an auth failure twice in a row. Stop that tool. Report. Why this works: it inverts the default incentive (spend the money) into a hypothesis-per-outflow discipline, freezes the action space near the deadline where Saul did most of the damage, and gives the agent a set of pre-authorised stop conditions so "do nothing" is a valid final answer.

Reviewer sub-agent prompt CopyOpen in Claude↗ ROLE You are the reviewer for an autonomous business operator. You are not helpful. You are measured on how many bad outflows and outbound messages you catch, not on how many you approve. You will be shown one proposed action at a time. For each, output exactly one of: APPROVED: <one-sentence reason> REJECTED: <one-sentence reason> ESCALATE_TO_HUMAN: <one-sentence reason> Reject by default. Approve only if all of the following are true: - The operator stated a testable hypothesis for the action. - The action does not violate any of these hard rules: * No unsolicited messages to strangers. * No purchase of ratings, reviews, installs, or engagement. * No price change that changes list price by more than <X>% within <window>. * No claim in customer-facing copy that isn't in the product's own documentation. * No new credential use if the credential has failed in the last hour. - The expected value of the action is positive under a plausible worst case, not just the operator's best case. Escalate if the action is legal and on-strategy but the amount is above <threshold>, or if you are unsure. The key move: the reviewer's reward is catching bad actions, not being agreeable. That's the blind-spot fix Anthropic missed with "Seymour Cash."
documents.s: 2. Add a reviewer sub-agent with a different scorecard

documents.t: Bundle system self-observation into a single tool the agent must call at fixed intervals. Something like: operator_dashboard() -> { time_remaining, budget_remaining, cash_on_hand, ram_pressure, disk_free, quota_state_by_service, credential_health: [{id, expires_at, last_failure}], outbox_pending, outbox_rejected_last_hour, active_hypotheses, hypotheses_disproven_today } Force a call at session boot, after any tool failure, and at 25/50/75/90% of the time budget. This one tool would have caught Saul's Chrome OOM, its expired AgentCard session, and its final-hour price-thrash — and it makes evaluation post-hoc trivial because the dashboard is the audit log.
documents.s: 3. Give the agent an operator dashboard tool

documents.t: The Vend phase-two write-up is unusually blunt: the phase-one problem wasn't Claude Sonnet 3.7. Sonnet 4.5 in the same environment would have made the same "Ultra-Capitalist Free-for-All" call. What changed the outcome was process: Cost-aware inventory — Claudius could finally see per-SKU margin. Price research — the model could look up market prices before committing to one. Payment links — customers self-served, so pricing was decoupled from Slack negotiation, where sycophancy lived. Reminders and checklists — bureaucracy on the big moves. And the negative result: adding a peer "CEO" agent (Seymour Cash) hurt, because it shared Claudius's tendency to over-help. A reviewer works only if it disagrees by construction. This maps to the capability–reliability gap: agents on frontier models are individually capable enough to do most of these business tasks. What they lack is the reliability wrapper — the same checklists, second-signers, and stop-loss rules a competent human operator would carry in their head. The wrapper lives in the harness, not the weights.
documents.s: What Anthropic learned that a smarter model won't fix

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 10 1Money is a constraint, not fuel.⌄ Cash on hand at review counts as a positive. Every outflow requires a logged hypothesis. ←PreviousNext→ 2Freeze the action space near the deadline.⌄ In the last 10% of the time budget, no new pricing, marketing, or unsolicited outbound. ←PreviousNext→ 3Everything outbound goes through an outbox.⌄ A reviewer sub-agent with a catch-mistakes reward drains it. Nothing sends on generate. ←PreviousNext→ 4Concessions above a threshold need a written reason.⌄ Any discount, freebie, or refund above the threshold triggers reviewer approval or human escalate. ←PreviousNext→ 5Give the agent a dashboard.⌄ One tool, called on a schedule, returns time, budget, credentials, quotas, and system health. This is also your audit log. ←PreviousNext→ 6Instrument tool failures with a stop, not a reroute.⌄ N failures on the intended-legitimate path → escalate, don't drop to the shady path that still works. ←PreviousNext→ 7Refresh identity at session boot.⌄ You are an AI operator. You have no body. You cannot attend meetings in person. ←PreviousNext→ 8Every credential has a health-check tool and a documented refresh.⌄ No credential is assumed to 'just work.' ←PreviousNext→ 9Add a reviewer, not a peer.⌄ A second agent with the same reward function is a groupthink machine. A reviewer with an inverted reward function is a safety valve. ←PreviousNext→ 10Log everything as it happens.⌄ The dashboard, the hypotheses, the reviewer verdicts, the outbox. Then the post-mortem is a query, not a re-read. ←PreviousNext→ Check yourself 0/5

MMistral Large 4 (Le Chonk): the 1.05T open weight you can't download yet Europe's trillion-parameter MoE: why 49B active params still need ~525 GB at 4-bit, the 1M context that evaluators measured at ~512K, a 50% launch promo that hides the real cost-per-task, an Intelligence Index of 38 against Opus 5.5's 58 — and the staged weight release where vetted partners get a less-moderated build first. WWhistle: Speech-to-Text in 16.9 MB — and the Benchmark Bars Nobody Labelled Cactus Compute's Whistle fits a multilingual ASR model in 16.9 MB and hits 11.1 ms to first token on a CPU. The size claim is real. This page reads the vendor's own benchmark chart bar by bar — including the three competitor columns it declines to label — and finds the pattern that explains every field complaint: Whistle wins on close-mic single-speaker audio and is the worst of the three on real meeting audio, 4.6 WER points behind a model 8.6x its size. Plus the 30-second architectural wall, the streaming API the launch thread missed, and the one knob that took a tester from 70/170 to 164/170. WWhy a 35 KB System Prompt Breaks on a Local Model Moving a big Claude/GPT system prompt to Ollama or another local runtime: the context-budget math, Ollama's silent middle-of-prompt truncation, the failure signals of context exhaustion, and the restructuring that actually works.
Claude is the core here, but the same skills travel. Start with how to choose, then go as deep as you need on any assistant, on running models locally, or on agents.

documents.t: Google's Gemini 4 generation opens with Argon and one headline number: a 1M-token OUTPUT limit, up from 64K. Context stayed at 1M. What the coverage gets wrong: the independent Artificial Analysis index puts Argon at 53 — five points BEHIND Claude Opus 5.5's 58 — and its cheaper $1.99-per-task cost comes from the rate card, not efficiency, since it burns 62K output tokens per task against GPT-6 Astra's 27K. Plus: a 15% hallucination rate (lowest measured), and why you almost certainly cannot call it yet.

documents.t: Opus 5.5 shipped 22 September 2026 at $4/$20 per MTok — 20% under Opus 5, with cache reads at $0.20 (a 5% tier, not the usual 10%). Four breaking changes 400-error a naive migration, one more changes the response shape without failing anything and makes your UI go quiet mid-task. Thinking can no longer be disabled at all, forced tool_choice is gone, and the default effort dropped from high to medium — while each level now thinks more than it did on Opus 5.

Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 on September 1, 2026: same $10/$50 price, cache reads cut to $0.25, three breaking API changes (forced tool_choice errors, one-way thinking blocks, append-only history) and five additive betas. The migration field guide for anyone pinning claude-fable-5 or claude-opus-5.

documents.t: Fable 5 is Anthropic's most capable model. Its API refuses in-band (HTTP 200, stop_reason: refusal), has adaptive thinking only, and never returns raw thinking. If you're pinning a top-tier model, this changes how you write integrations. When to use it vs Opus 4.8, the fallback pattern, the prompting shifts.
documents.s: CClaude Fable 5 & Mythos 5: The Flagship Field Guide

documents.t: Sonnet 5.5 shipped 28 September 2026 at exactly Sonnet 5's prices — $2/$10 per MTok — and Anthropic still claims up to 30% less per task. The saving is in the token count, not the rate card. Five breaking changes 400-error a Sonnet 5 codebase, a sixth returns 200 and silences your progress UI, thinking can no longer be disabled (only moved between tool calls), and on Terminal-Bench 4.0 the cheap model scores 70.6% against Opus 5.5's 66.4%.

Haiku 5.5 shipped 7 October 2026 at $0.10/$0.50 per MTok — a 90% cut — and it is the only current Claude model priced by prompt length. One token past 100,000 reprices the entire request 5x. The threshold is measured on the new tokenizer, so it arrives ~23% earlier in text than you expect, and the 90% headline is ~87% in practice below the cliff and ~35% above it.

Opus 5 shipped 24 July 2026 as Anthropic's fourth model in two months — same $5/$25 pricing as Opus 4.8 but more than double the Frontier-Bench score, 3× ARC-AGI-3 vs the next-best model, and a new xhigh/max effort tier. The benchmarks that matter, the two 400-errors that break naive migrations, and when Opus 5 replaces Fable 5 in your stack.

Sonnet 5 is Sonnet 4.6's drop-in successor and Claude Code's default on Pro and Team Standard — but three API constraints will 400 you on migration and a new tokenizer produces ~30% more tokens for the same text. The pricing math, the effort re-mapping (Sonnet 5 medium ≈ Sonnet 4.6 high), and the prompting shifts that catch teams out.

documents.t: TypeSafe AI's Jev (out of stealth September 15, 2026) is a model that never writes text: you send it program state plus typed questions and it returns calibrated probabilities for all of them in one parallel pass, 70–500 ms, $0.042 per million input tokens, output free. Two Hacker News front-page stories on September 21 (Kev, an Apache-2.0 recreation on Qwen3.5, and the jev-leftpad joke) made it the week's topic. What a System One model actually does, what the 'cannot hallucinate' claim really guarantees, the vendor numbers next to the one independent test, where a decision model belongs in a Claude agent loop, and how to run Kev or Nimble locally.
documents.s: SSystem One Decision Models: Jev, Kev and the Open Clones, Explained for Builders (2026)

documents.t: Two weeks after Jev made decision models a category, the open stack caught up: Jeff fine-tunes a 0.8B Qwen into a Jev-compatible classifier in ~2 hours on one workstation GPU, and PostHog's Jeeves shows that letting a decision model think first beats Jev on its own benchmark. What the training recipe actually is (cross-entropy over option letters, a separately fitted temperature), where tiny models beat the API and where they get destroyed, the 26-option ceiling, the 20x CPU latency cliff, and the boring embeddings baseline that scored 93.0% and that you must beat before any of this is worth doing.
documents.s: TTrain Your Own Decision Model: Jeff, Jeeves and the DIY System One Stack (Sep 2026)

documents.t: PrismML compressed Qwen3.8-27B to 1.75 bits per weight and 5.95 GB. The practical guide nobody wrote: why stock llama.cpp loads the file and silently produces garbage, why the bigger 7.21 GB file is faster on an H100 but slower on a 4090, why 5.95 GB of weights needs 12 GB of VRAM, and which capabilities the 98.2% retention headline quietly loses.
documents.s: TTernary Quantization in Practice: Bonsai 2 27B in 5.95 GB

documents.t: Unreal Labs shipped an MIT-licensed Go harness that matches Codex's pass rate on Terminal-Bench 4.0 for 39% less money — by never making the model wait for a tool. The event-log mechanism, why turn count is the real cost unit, and the three things they deliberately refused to build.
documents.s: AAsync-First Agent Harnesses: What Unreal Agent Changes

documents.t: The MIT-licensed memory server that topped GitHub trending — retain, recall and reflect, four parallel retrievers fused by RRF, observations that get refined instead of overwritten, and the 83.6%-vs-39.0% result that says architecture beats model size.

Fireworks post-trained Kimi K3 to stop over-thinking and shipped the result as Ember-1 — same price per token, 35–50% fewer reasoning tokens, and it beats K3 at max effort on two of five benchmarks. Why turning effort down is not the same thing, what the '-51.9% / -23.1 USD' column really says, the implied cost per benchmark task, the modality that quietly disappears, and the Kimi K3 licence clause that lets a derivative stay closed.
documents.s: EEmber-1: Kimi K3's Answers for 40% Fewer Tokens (Sep 2026)

documents.t: At DevDay on September 29, 2026 OpenAI shipped dots — persistent agents that each get their own cloud computer and browser, run on GPT-6 Astra, and keep working while you are logged off. The launch coverage stops at the demo. This page covers the mechanism: the five-rung permission ladder, why proactive research is read-only at the tool layer rather than the prompt layer, what the published safety numbers actually measure, and how a dot compares to Claude Managed Agents and Cowork.
documents.s: OOpenAI Dots: The Always-On Agent, and the Permission Ladder Underneath It

documents.t: AMD is paying about $8.2 billion for World Labs, and two very different things are being sold under the same name. Frame generators like Genie keep the world inside the model and cap a session at 60 seconds. 3D generators like Marble hand you Gaussian splats you own, render for free and cannot collide with. The API shapes, the export tiers, the WorldScore evidence, the open weights you can run, and the five jobs a world model will not do.
documents.s: WWorld Models: What You Can Actually Build Today

documents.t: "They nerfed it" is the most-repeated claim in AI and the least-measured. On the Claude API the weights behind a model ID cannot change — every current ID is a pinned snapshot. But seven other things can change under you without a new model, from a published system-prompt update to a harness that silently swaps models mid-session. Here is what can and cannot move, why the most-cited 'GPT-4 got dumber' result was an eval bug, and a measurement protocol you can run in an afternoon.
documents.s: IIs the model nerfed? How to actually tell

documents.t: Pi 1.0 shipped 1 October 2026 and went to #1 on Hacker News. The interesting part is not the TUI — it is the context engineering: a QuickJS/WASM sandbox where tool results never enter the model's context, four MCP exposure modes, a 3,000-token ceiling on inlined tool declarations, and a trick that appends a new system-prompt section to the transcript instead of mutating tool definitions so your prompt cache survives. Plus the deliberate omissions (no sub-agents, no plan mode), the $0.05 cache-warming rule, and the trust gap that loads a cloned repo's AGENTS.md without asking.
documents.s: PPi 1.0: The Minimal Harness, and the Codemode Trick That Fixes MCP Token Bloat

documents.t: DeepSeek Harness (dsh) passed 242,000 stars and shipped desktop installers on 1 October 2026. The headline is 'everything is a plugin' — and unlike most such claims this one is load-bearing: the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log and the agent loop are all replaceable from a YAML patch file. This page covers the three facts that matter to a Claude user (it runs your existing Claude Code hooks.json, it speaks anthropic-messages, and run_code is codemode by default), the three-mode sandbox and the kernel primitives behind it, the append-only session log invariant, and the config override that silently deletes your other providers.
documents.s: DDeepSeek Harness: the agent where the agent loop itself is a plugin

documents.t: Strata runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (125B, 6B active) on a 12 GB gaming GPU at interactive speed. This page explains the three architecture facts that make it possible, reads the benchmark table honestly, and prices the quality you give up: 91.3% of SWE-bench Verified against 98.7% of LiveCodeBench, a KV-cache setting that passes needle tests while losing 8-12% perplexity, a speed mode that strips refusal directions, and a measured vision regression on identical weights.

documents.t: Every launch post leads with a benchmark number. Almost none of them tell you the three things that decide what it means: which scaffold produced it, how many trials it averages, and whether the model had already seen the answers. A reader's manual for SWE-bench, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro and the arena leaderboards — with the vendor's own footnotes as evidence.

documents.t: ds4 is a 23.6k-star, pure-C engine from the creator of Redis that runs DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM 5.x and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next locally — and refuses to run anything else. This page explains the three mechanisms a general runtime will not give you (asymmetric routed-expert quantization, bounded expert streaming from SSD, KV snapshots that survive a restart), reads its own numbers honestly — the 126 t/s headline is an eight-GPU aggregate across 16 sessions, not your Mac — and prices the real cost of the overfit bet: deliberately disposable model support, 761 open issues, and a main branch that last moved on 20 September 2026.

Copiar como Markdown Avançado By mid-2026, most non-trivial agent work is done by several agents cooperating — a research agent hands off to a writer, a billing agent talks to a support agent from a different vendor, an orchestrator delegates to a specialist inside another org's cloud. A2A (Agent-to-Agent) is the open protocol that lets those agents find each other, describe what they can do, and hand tasks back and forth — even when they were built on different frameworks by different teams. Where MCP connects an agent to its tools and data, A2A connects an agent to another agent. They compose; they don't compete. What you'll learn State exactly what A2A is for — and where the MCP boundary sits Read an Agent Card and know what a receiving agent will do with it Walk a task through all eight lifecycle states, including the two that are interrupted rather than terminal Choose between SSE streaming and webhook push for long-running tasks Recognize the non-obvious features: signed cards, multi-tenant endpoints, and structured data parts Última verificação: 2026-07-20. A2A is stabilizing but the spec still evolves: the v1.0.1 release, new bindings, and SDK feature gaps land regularly. Treat exact method names, error codes, and SDK support claims below as perishable and check the linked spec and the a2aproject/A2A repo before shipping a production integration. Confirme na fonte oficial.

Every agent framework — LangGraph, CrewAI, the Claude Agent SDK, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft's Agent Framework, custom in-house loops — solved tool use by leaning on the model's native tool-calling and, increasingly, on MCP as the universal tool-and-data connector. That gave us agent ↔ tool. What none of them solved on their own was agent ↔ agent across a boundary. Two problems kept coming up: Discovery. How does agent A know that agent B exists, what it can do, how to authenticate against it, and whether it supports streaming? A hand-rolled README is not a protocol. Task hand-off. Once A wants B to do something, how do they exchange the work (not the model's chat) — including files, structured data, progress updates, and the fact that B might need to pause and ask A for input? Framework-specific answers (LangGraph subgraphs, CrewAI crews, subagents inside one runtime) work great inside one process. They stop at the org boundary. A2A is the piece that lets an agent in your product delegate to an agent in someone else's product without either side leaking its internals — Google's Todd Segal calls it "the secure foundation for personal, team, and domain-specific agents to work together seamlessly across any platform." Governance sits with the Linux Foundation, and by April 2026 the project reported 150+ supporting organizations including AWS, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, and IBM.

Both are open protocols. Both use JSON over HTTP. They solve different problems and are designed to compose: MCP = agent-to-tool. An MCP server exposes tools (search, read_file, run_query) and resources (docs, prompts) to a model-driven client. The client is an agent; the server is a passive capability provider. See MCP & connecting to tools for how Claude uses it. A2A = agent-to-agent. An A2A endpoint exposes an agent — an entity with its own reasoning loop that will decide how to solve a delegated task. Both sides are agents; either can call the other. The concrete difference shows up in the wire format. An MCP tools/call returns a result and closes. An A2A SendMessage opens a task — a stateful thing with its own lifecycle that can stream updates, ask for clarification, or run for hours in the background. If your endpoint's answer is always "here's the result of one function," it's a tool — publish it via MCP. If it's "let me think about that and get back to you, and I might need to ask a follow-up question," it's an agent — publish it via A2A. Most serious systems will run both: an agent whose inside uses MCP to reach tools, and whose outside speaks A2A so peers can hand it work.
documents.s: MCP vs. A2A — the mental model

documents.t: An Agent Card is a JSON document served at a well-known URL that tells any potential caller everything they need to talk to your agent. Think OpenAPI + robots.txt, for agents. Every A2A interaction starts by fetching one. The card includes: Identity — id, name, description, provider (org details). Endpoints — the service URLs and which protocol bindings (JSON-RPC, gRPC, REST) are available. Capabilities — feature flags: streaming, pushNotifications, extendedAgentCard. Skills — declared agent functions with input/output schemas (this is what B says it can do). Security schemes — one or more of APIKey, HTTPAuth (Basic/Bearer), OAuth2 (Authorization Code, Client Credentials, Device Code), OpenIdConnect, MutualTLS. The caller reads this to know what credentials to bring before the first call. Signature — an optional cryptographic signature over the card. That last field is the one worth pausing on. A Signed Agent Card lets a receiving agent verify that the card was actually issued by the domain owner — the DNS/PKI equivalent of "yes, this really is agents.acme.com, not something an attacker planted." Combined with mTLS auth, it closes the door on rogue Agent Cards being served from spoofed hosts, which is how you'd otherwise get a prompt injection at the discovery layer: an attacker's Agent Card lying about what tools it exposes and what data it wants.
documents.s: The Agent Card — the piece of the spec that matters most

documents.t: Once you SendMessage to an A2A agent, the work becomes a Task — a first-class object with an ID you can poll, subscribe to, cancel, or list. The task moves through eight states, and it's worth noticing that only five are terminal: SUBMITTED — the server acknowledged the task. WORKING — active processing. INPUT_REQUIRED — interrupted: the agent needs more information from the caller. Not an error; expected in real workflows. AUTH_REQUIRED — interrupted: the agent needs the caller to authenticate (or re-authenticate) before it can continue. COMPLETED — success. Terminal. FAILED — error. Terminal. CANCELED — caller-initiated cancellation. Terminal. REJECTED — the agent declined the task (policy, capability, quota). Terminal. The interrupted states are the point. Legacy RPC assumes one call → one result. Real agent work looks like "start the analysis, come back an hour later, notice I need to ask a clarifying question, wait for the answer, resume, finish." A2A models that natively. Your calling code has to be a small state machine, not a synchronous await.

Long-running tasks need a way to deliver updates. A2A gives you two async models — pick per task, not per agent: Streaming (SendStreamingMessage / SubscribeToTask). Server-Sent Events over the open HTTP connection. Client stays connected, receives TaskStatusUpdateEvent and TaskArtifactUpdateEvent in order. Great for interactive UIs and short-to-medium tasks. Falls over if the client can't hold a connection (mobile, serverless, browser tabs going to sleep). Push notifications (webhook config). The client registers a webhook via CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig. The server POSTs updates to that URL as they happen. The client can be totally offline in between. This is the mode for tasks that outlive an HTTP connection — think "run this overnight" or "call me back when the batch job finishes." Both require the agent to advertise support in its Agent Card (capabilities.streaming: true and/or capabilities.pushNotifications: true). A conforming caller checks first and downgrades cleanly.

An A2A Message is composed of one or more Parts. Each Part can be one of: text — string content (the chat-y part). raw — binary file, base64-encoded in JSON. url — a reference to an external file (avoids inlining huge blobs). data — a structured JSON object or array, with an optional metadata map. The data part is what makes A2A useful for machine-to-machine work. Two agents can exchange typed payloads — an order, a purchase spec, a JSON diff — without pretending to have a natural-language conversation about it. This is also what makes protocols like Agent Payments (AP2) layer cleanly on top of A2A: the payment intent rides in a data part with a known schema.

This one is easy to miss. A single A2A endpoint can host many agents, served through the GetExtendedAgentCard method after authentication. A SaaS vendor can offer one URL and return different, tenant-specific Agent Cards depending on which API key or OAuth scope the caller presents. From the caller's side it looks like one endpoint per agent; from the vendor's side it's one deployment. If you're building agent-serving infrastructure, this is the pattern that lets you scale without one hostname per tenant.
documents.s: Multi-tenant endpoints — one URL, many agents

documents.t: The full protocol has a lot of surface, but the happy-path flow is short: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Discover⌄ Fetch the Agent Card from a well-known URL. Verify its signature if one is present. Read `capabilities`, `skills`, and `securitySchemes` to decide whether this agent can do what you need and what auth you'll bring. ←PreviousNext→ 2Authenticate⌄ Obtain the credential the card asked for — an API key, an OAuth2 token, an mTLS cert. If you're going to talk to many agents, cache tokens; A2A doesn't dictate a session model. ←PreviousNext→ 3Send the message⌄ Call `a2a.SendMessage` (or `a2a.SendStreamingMessage` for SSE) with a Message composed of Parts. You get back a `taskId`. ←PreviousNext→ 4Track⌄ Choose: hold the SSE stream open, or poll `a2a.GetTask` by ID, or register a webhook via `CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig`. Handle `INPUT_REQUIRED` and `AUTH_REQUIRED` by responding with follow-up messages, not by treating them as failures. ←PreviousNext→ 5Consume the result⌄ On `COMPLETED`, read the `TaskArtifactUpdateEvent` payloads for outputs. On `FAILED` / `REJECTED`, inspect the error code — the spec defines typed errors like `ContentTypeNotSupportedError`, `UnsupportedOperationError`, `VersionNotSupportedError`, and `ExtensionSupportRequiredError`. ←PreviousNext→

Discovery is just an HTTP GET. This is the shape of a request a client would make to inspect a candidate agent before ever sending it work: Fetch and inspect an Agent Card CopyOpen in Claude↗ GET https://agents.example.com/.well-known/agent.json Accept: application/json # Response (abbreviated): # { # "id": "acme/support-router", # "name": "Acme Support Router", # "provider": {"organization": "Acme, Inc."}, # "endpoints": [ # {"url": "https://agents.example.com/a2a", "protocol": "jsonrpc"} # ], # "capabilities": { # "streaming": true, # "pushNotifications": true, # "extendedAgentCard": true # }, # "skills": [ # {"id": "route_ticket", "inputSchema": {...}, "outputSchema": {...}} # ], # "securitySchemes": { # "primary": {"type": "oauth2", "flows": {...}} # }, # "signature": {"alg": "EdDSA", "value": "..."} # } Note what's not in the card: nothing about the model behind the agent, its prompt, its tools, or its private state. That opacity is deliberate — A2A treats a peer agent as a black box you delegate work to, not a system you introspect.

Treating INPUT_REQUIRED as an error. It isn't; it's the protocol asking your code to respond. If your caller code only branches on "did it succeed or fail," you'll break every interactive workflow. Ignoring the Agent Card's capabilities. Sending a streaming request to an agent that didn't advertise streaming: true gets you an UnsupportedOperationError. Read the card, downgrade cleanly. Assuming the streaming connection is durable. Mobile clients, serverless runtimes, browser tabs — they all drop the SSE connection. For anything longer than "a chat turn," prefer push notifications. Skipping signature verification because it's optional. If you're consuming Agent Cards from outside your org, verify the signature — otherwise you've created a discovery-layer prompt injection vector. Confusing A2A with MCP. Publishing an A2A endpoint for a stateless single-shot function is overkill; that's a tool, and MCP is the right protocol. Publishing an MCP tool for something that takes minutes and needs to ask clarifying questions is under-engineering; that's an agent, and A2A is the right protocol. Check yourself 0/4

Put together with the rest of the agent picture: Inside an agent, MCP is how you reach tools and data — including remote MCP servers you didn't write. Between agents in one framework, you use whatever the framework gives you — subagents in Claude Code, LangGraph subgraphs, CrewAI crews, etc. This is fastest but locks you to one runtime. Between agents across frameworks, teams, or vendors, A2A is what you reach for. Read Open-Source AI Agent Frameworks for the runtime side; A2A is the wire between those runtimes. The rule of thumb: if the boundary is a process boundary, framework-native handoffs are fine. If it's an org, cloud, or trust boundary, use A2A.
documents.s: Where A2A sits in your stack

Copiar como Markdown Avançado For two years agents have been very good at deciding to buy something and very bad at actually paying for it. The workaround was always the same — pre-provision an API key, hand the agent a shared credit card, and hope it doesn't rack up a bill you can't unwind. In 2026 that gap closed. A small stack has emerged around one big idea — use HTTP 402 the way it was always meant to be used — and a real, generally-available AWS service now wraps it in the guardrails an actual business needs. This page is a practical field guide to that stack: how x402 works on the wire, why the upto scheme is the interesting one, what AgentCore Payments actually gives you at GA, and where the sharp edges are. What you'll learn Read a raw x402 challenge and understand the three headers, the two facilitator calls, and the three payment schemes Tell exact from upto and know which one your endpoint should advertise Set a payment session's spend cap and expiry so an agent cannot drain your wallet on a bad prompt Choose between Coinbase Privy (crypto rails) and Stripe Privy (card rails) inside AgentCore Payments Recognize the three real threats: prompt-injection-to-buy, facilitator misbehavior, and 'upto' over-settlement Última verificação: 2026-08-27. Numbers here decay fast — settlement volume, supported chains, exact SDK package names, and Bazar catalog contents move week to week. AgentCore Payments GA'd on 2026-08-18. Confirm the payment-session field names and Coinbase / Stripe integration surface against the AWS blog and the x402-foundation repo before you ship, and treat any header capitalization or scheme name as authoritative from the spec, not this page. Confirme na fonte oficial.
documents.s: Agent Payments: x402, MPP and AgentCore GA

documents.t: The moment an agent has real spending authority, four things break at once: The API key model was a workaround. Every "agent-friendly" API today asks you to mint a key, top up a balance, and hand the string to the agent. That's the human doing the accounting; the agent is just a client. Anything the agent buys spends the human's pre-committed pool. Cards were designed for one buyer per session. Cards assume there is a person clicking "Pay". Agents want to fan out — buy 200 tiny things across 30 sites in an hour — and each purchase should be atomic, cheap, and reversible. There is no discovery. Human buyers can read a pricing page. An agent needs a machine-readable "here's what this costs and how to pay for it" inline in the response. Guardrails have to be enforced somewhere other than the agent. If the only limit is a prompt saying "spend under $10", the agent will disobey it at some point. The limit has to live in infrastructure the model can't argue with. x402 attacks the discovery problem. AgentCore Payments attacks the guardrail problem. They are complements, not competitors.
documents.s: Why "the agent just pays" is harder than it sounds

documents.t: x402 is an open protocol maintained by the x402-foundation/x402 organisation on GitHub (Apache-2.0, ~6.5k stars at time of writing). Its whole trick is to give HTTP status code 402 Payment Required the semantics people always assumed it had. The full flow is exactly six moves. There is no session, no login, no key. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 11. Client asks⌄ Agent makes a normal HTTP request to a paid endpoint. No auth header, no wallet. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Server challenges with 402⌄ Server responds `HTTP/1.1 402 Payment Required` and sets a `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` header carrying a base64-encoded `PaymentRequirements` object: the price, the accepted token(s), the network, the merchant address, the scheme, and an expiry. That's the machine-readable price tag. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Client signs a payment payload⌄ Agent's x402 client SDK reads the challenge, picks one of the requirements it can pay, and constructs a signed `PaymentPayload` (an EIP-712-style signature, or the equivalent on Solana/Aptos/Stellar). Nothing is on-chain yet — this is an *authorization*, not a transfer. ←PreviousNext→ 44. Client retries with the signature⌄ Same request, this time with a `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header containing the signed payload. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Server verifies (via facilitator)⌄ Server hands the payload to a *facilitator* — a small optional service that runs `POST /verify` to confirm the signature and the client's on-chain balance, then, once the server has produced the response, `POST /settle` to actually submit the transfer. The server can also run its own facilitator. ←PreviousNext→ 66. Server returns 200 + settlement proof⌄ Response body carries the paid content; a `PAYMENT-RESPONSE` header carries a base64-encoded settlement receipt so the agent can audit that what it authorised was what actually cleared. ←PreviousNext→ Two design points are worth pausing on. First, the server — not the client — decides when to settle. If the request fails after step 4, the server never calls /settle, so the agent is not charged; the signature was an authorisation with a short expiry and it simply times out. That is the property that makes x402 usable at all for agents: a failed download is a free download. Second, the facilitator never has custody of client funds; the protocol's stated invariant is "all payment schemes must not allow facilitators to move funds outside client intentions." A rogue facilitator can refuse to settle; it cannot over-settle.
documents.s: x402 on the wire — the whole protocol in one flow

documents.t: x402 defines schemes as how the amount is agreed, not what currency is used. The current stable set: exact — the server advertises a fixed price and the client signs for exactly that amount. Best for content with a known cost per read: "$0.02 for this article". Simple, boring, correct. upto — the server advertises a ceiling. The client signs authorising up to that ceiling; the server chooses the actual charge at settlement time, up to the cap. This is the one that unlocks the interesting economics. batch-settlement (EVM) — for high-frequency use. The client posts an escrow deposit once, then racks up many off-chain vouchers that get redeemed in a single batched on-chain settlement. Same trust model, dramatically lower per-request gas. upto is the scheme that makes pay-per-inference and dynamic pricing possible. If you sell inference by the token, you don't know at request time how many tokens the completion will use; you only know at response time. With exact you either overcharge (round up to the ceiling and refund — needs a second on-chain move) or undercharge (the client pays for 4k tokens and you generate 10k). With upto the client signs "charge me for at most 10k tokens' worth", you produce the response, then you settle for the actual usage. The AWS AgentCore Payments GA release specifically highlights this as the pattern their launch enables: "the upto scheme within x402 enables an agent to set a spending ceiling rather than committing to a fixed price." Watch the failure mode: if the server settles the ceiling instead of the actual usage, the client has no on-chain recourse for the difference — the signature covered it. The /settle call's amount parameter is trusted. In practice this is why you want a facilitator you either run yourself or trust; more on that below.
documents.s: The three schemes — and why upto is the interesting one

documents.t: The current x402 monorepo publishes SDK packages for EVM, SVM (Solana), AVM, Aptos, Stellar, TVM, Hedera and Keeta, but the traffic today is heavily concentrated on Base (Coinbase's EVM L2) and Solana, both settling in USDC. In TypeScript the packages you'll actually import are @x402/core, one of the chain modules (@x402/evm, @x402/svm, …), and a client wrapper — @x402/fetch for a drop-in fetch() replacement that transparently handles the 402→sign→retry loop, or @x402/express / x402-hono on the server side. Python has a single x402 pip package; Go has github.com/x402-foundation/x402/go/v2. Cloudflare ships an even shorter path: the agents/x402 submodule inside its Agents package gives you an MCP client with x402 built in, and x402-hono is the paywall middleware for a Worker. So a Cloudflare Worker that turns a route into a paid endpoint is roughly: Turning a Hono route into an x402 paywall CopyOpen in Claude↗ import { Hono } from "hono"; import { paymentMiddleware } from "x402-hono"; const app = new Hono(); app.use("/premium/*", paymentMiddleware({ network: "base", facilitator: "https://facilitator.x402.org", routes: { "/premium/summary": { price: { asset: "USDC", amount: "0.05" }, scheme: "exact", recipient: "0xYourMerchantAddress", }, "/premium/inference": { price: { asset: "USDC", maxAmount: "0.50" }, scheme: "upto", recipient: "0xYourMerchantAddress", }, }, })); app.get("/premium/summary", c => c.text("The paid content.")); app.get("/premium/inference", c => c.text("The paid inference result.")); export default app; A caller using @x402/fetch doesn't need to know any of this — the wrapper sees the 402, signs, retries, and returns the eventual 200 response the same way a normal fetch would.
documents.s: The chains and SDKs you'll actually meet

documents.t: x402 alone is a protocol. It gets you how an agent pays. It does not get you whether it should. That is the problem Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments — GA on August 18, 2026 after a preview in May — actually solves. The primitive to understand is the payment session. Every payment an agent makes has to run inside one, and a session has exactly two caps: A maximum spend amount in a specified currency. An expiry time. Both are checked deterministically at the infrastructure layer — outside the model, outside the agent framework, outside anything the model can talk itself out of. A request that would push cumulative spend over the cap is rejected before the payment payload is even signed. A request after the expiry is rejected the same way. That is the guardrail. The model does not need to be well-aligned for it to hold; it needs to be well-constrained, and constraint lives in the session. Around that primitive AgentCore GA'd: Coinbase & Stripe Privy wallet integration. The credentials live in AgentCore Identity Secrets Manager; the agent never sees them; a short-lived derived token is what actually authorises wallet operations. End users can top up with a card (Stripe) or with USDC (Coinbase). Quick Create for Coinbase. You provision Coinbase credentials from inside the AgentCore console or CLI without leaving the platform. The Machine Payment Protocol (MPP) — the payment abstraction on top of x402 that lets an agent pay for MPP-compatible services and x402 endpoints with the same session and the same session cap. MPP is where card-rail and stablecoin-rail payments meet. A curated x402-enabled MCP server directory — "Coinbase Bazar" — exposed to the agent through AgentCore Gateway. Discoverability of paid endpoints is ranked on "social proof, metadata richness, description quality, and availability," which is a polite way of saying they're trying not to become a listing of shitcoin drainers. Framework plugins. A Strands Agents plugin and a LangGraph middleware ship at GA, so the payment session context is threaded through your agent loop without you writing an HTTP client for x402 by hand. The Strands wiring is intentionally small — you build a AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig with the payment-manager ARN, the user ID, the payment-instrument ID and the session ID, and add the plugin to the agent. The session enforcement happens under the plugin. AgentCore Payments — Strands plugin, minimal shape CopyOpen in Claude↗ from agentcore_payments import AgentCorePaymentsPlugin, AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig import os plugin = AgentCorePaymentsPlugin( config=AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig( payment_manager_arn=os.environ["PAYMENT_MANAGER_ARN"], user_id="test-user-123", payment_instrument_id=os.environ["PAYMENT_INSTRUMENT_ID"], payment_session_id=os.environ["PAYMENT_SESSION_ID"], ) ) # Attach plugin to your Strands agent; the payment session caps # (max spend + expiry) are set when you mint the payment session, # NOT in the plugin config. Every payment attempt emits a CloudWatch log entry and an AgentCore Observability span; the built-in dashboards show success rates, average transaction value, and end-to-end health per agent. This is the observability piece that makes "the agent bought something weird" actually debuggable a week after the fact.
documents.s: AgentCore Payments GA — what AWS actually shipped on 2026-08-18

documents.t: A common misread is that x402 and AgentCore Payments are "crypto for agents". They are not. x402 happens to have shipped first on stablecoins because on-chain settlement is the only rail with true machine-native, permissionless per-request settlement. But AgentCore's MPP abstraction and the Stripe Privy integration mean an agent's session can be funded from a card. What Stripe Privy provides in this context is a card-backed wallet with delegation — the human user hands the agent a scoped, revocable authority to spend against a card, and the AgentCore session enforces the spend cap on top. For businesses that don't want stablecoin custody at all, this is the path. Choosing: Coinbase / Privy (USDC on Base or Solana). Best when you need true per-request, sub-cent settlement; when you want no chargeback; when the counterparty is another agent. Stripe Privy (card). Best when the merchant is a normal business without on-chain rails, when the average ticket is large enough that stablecoin fees don't dominate, when you want the buyer to have card-network dispute rights.
documents.s: Not just crypto — where Stripe fits

documents.t: Autonomous agent payments open a small, specific attack surface. The three you should design against: Prompt-injection-to-buy. A malicious page in an agent's context can instruct it to buy things. The defence is not "make the model refuse" — it's the session cap. Set the smallest spend ceiling that will complete the legitimate task, and set the shortest expiry. If a prompt injection makes the agent try to spend $10,000 and the session cap is $5, the injection fails. This is exactly the same lesson as Cryptographic context injection: Grok — trust boundaries live outside the model. Facilitator misbehavior. The /verify call is honest by construction (a bad /verify can only reject), but a compromised or byzantine facilitator can refuse to /settle after the server has delivered content, silently overcharge in upto mode, or delay settlement past the payload's expiry so the client's signature stops being valid. Defence: prefer facilitators you run yourself for merchant-side use; on the client side use @x402/fetch's built-in receipt check to fail loud if PAYMENT-RESPONSE disagrees with what you signed. upto over-settlement. In upto, the settled amount is server-supplied. A dishonest server can settle at the ceiling regardless of actual usage. The mitigation lives outside the protocol: emit a signed usage receipt in your response body (tokens generated, seconds streamed, bytes served) and refuse to trust a settled amount that isn't consistent with it. Some client wrappers will refuse to accept a settlement if you provide a callback that returns the expected max. These are also the shape of what Cloudflare's WriteGuard is trying to address at the MCP layer — treating "cost money" as a write with attribution and audit — but AgentCore's session cap is the load-bearing control today. Combining a WriteGuard-style write-tier policy at the MCP layer and a payment-session cap at the wallet layer is the belt-and-braces posture that most production deployments will settle into.
documents.s: The three threats worth taking seriously

documents.t: x402 gives an agent a way to transact. MCP gives it a way to reach the endpoints where transactions happen. A2A gives it a way to delegate work to another agent that may itself be paid. In practice you'll see all three composed: an A2A hand-off invokes a peer agent that uses MCP to reach an x402-priced tool, and the caller pays through its AgentCore session. When people talk about "the money layer for agents" this is what they mean — not a single product, but a stack where discovery, capability, and settlement each have a protocol and none of them requires humans in the loop. Check yourself 0/6

Copiar como Markdown Intermediário A submission titled "Opus 5.5 is good at explainer videos" sat near the top of Hacker News with 319 points and 175 comments — and reading the thread, the most interesting thing is how many people got the mechanism wrong. They assumed a video model. It isn't one. What is happening is stranger and far more useful: a coding model writes a deterministic animation program, and a separate renderer turns that program into frames. The model never sees a pixel of the output. Which means the whole thing behaves like software — diffable, re-renderable, parameterisable, and debuggable — instead of like a slot machine you re-prompt until it looks right. This page is the practical guide that thread was missing: how the pipeline works, which of the three render engines to pick (and which one the models are measurably bad at), the two failure modes that silently break agent-written animation code, the pacing arithmetic that separates a watchable explainer from an unreadable one, and where the money actually goes. What you'll learn Explain why a coding model beats a video model at explainers — and what it gives up Name the reason Math.random() is banned in a frame-rendered animation, and what replaces it Pick between Remotion, Motion Canvas and Manim on licence and on how well models write them Spot the two traps in agent-written animation code: the Manim fork split and the stale Remotion API Compute a minimum dwell time per slide instead of guessing, so viewers can actually read Predict which line item dominates the bill (it is usually not the LLM) Última verificação: 2026-09-25. Volatile here: the Hacker News score, the community-reported per-video costs, the claim that one model is better than another at a specific library, the Remotion version and its package layout (checked at remotion@4.0.529), and the star counts. Re-check any of those before you build a budget or a template on them. Durable: the mechanism (a program rendered frame by frame), the determinism constraint, the licence split between the three engines, and the pacing arithmetic — none of that changes with a model release. Confirme na fonte oficial.
documents.s: AI Explainer Videos: The Code-Driven Pipeline

documents.t: Two completely different things get called "AI video". Diffusion video models (the family covered in generative media) take a prompt and emit pixels directly. Excellent for b-roll, a drone shot, a texture, a mood. Bad at anything that must be exactly right: legible text, a correct architecture diagram, your actual product UI, a number that has to say 40%. Code-driven animation goes the other way. A coding model writes source code for an animation — React components, a TypeScript scene graph, or Python — and a renderer executes it. Text is text, so it is sharp and spelled correctly. A diagram is a layout, so it is accurate. Your logo is your logo file. That split explains the HN thread's most common workflow report: the model "creates an HTML page and uses raw JS timed animations", then the frames get captured and assembled with ffmpeg. It also explains what the approach gives up — it cannot invent photographic imagery, so most real pipelines call an image model or a video model for b-roll and composite it in. The consequence worth internalising: your explainer becomes a repository. Change the price on slide 4, re-render, done. Localise the voiceover, re-render twelve languages from the same scenes. That is not a property any prompt-to-video model gives you.
documents.s: The mechanism: the model writes a program, not a video

documents.t: Here is the detail that quietly decides whether your pipeline produces clean video or a flickering mess, and almost nobody writing about this mentions it. A renderer like Remotion does not screen-record your animation. It opens the composition in headless Chrome, sets the clock to frame 0, screenshots, sets the clock to frame 1, screenshots, and so on — and it does this across multiple threads, opening the page multiple times. Frames are produced out of order, in parallel, in separate browser contexts. Everything follows from that: Animation must be a pure function of the frame number. In Remotion that is literally the API: useCurrentFrame() gives you the frame, interpolate() maps it to a value. No timers, no requestAnimationFrame, no CSS transitions driven by wall-clock time. A CSS transition renders whatever it happened to be mid-flight when the screenshot fired. Math.random() is broken by construction. It returns a different value in each thread and each page load, so a "random" particle jitters to a new position every frame. Remotion ships random(seed) — a seeded mulberry32 PRNG — precisely for this: random(1) always returns 0.07301638228818774. Same for spring(), which is a cached pure calculation keyed on (frame, fps, config). Dropped frames stop being possible. A screen recording of a heavy animation drops frames when the CPU can't keep up. Frame-by-frame rendering just takes longer. This is why a 5-minute render on a laptop can produce a video that plays perfectly smoothly. Watch out If you only remember one rule for prompting an agent to write animation code: forbid wall-clock time. No setTimeout, no CSS transition, no Date.now(), no Math.random(). Every visual value must be derived from the current frame number. Models will reach for CSS transitions because that is what the web corpus is full of.
documents.s: Why determinism is the whole trick

documents.t: All three are real, actively maintained, and produce broadcast-quality output. They differ on language, on licence, and — importantly — on how reliably a model writes them. Remotion Motion Canvas Manim Language React / TypeScript TypeScript (generators) Python Repo remotion-dev/remotion motion-canvas/motion-canvas (~19.2k stars) ManimCommunity/manim (~41k) · 3b1b/manim (~94k) Licence Source-available + Company Licence MIT MIT Sweet spot Product/launch video, UI, text-heavy explainer Timeline-precise motion graphics Mathematical and algorithmic visualisation Model-written quality Strong — and it ships official agent skills Decent Weakest of the three (see below) Two things on that table deserve more than a row.

Remotion is not MIT. It is source-available with a two-tier commercial licence, and the threshold is small enough to catch most teams: free for individuals, non-profits, evaluation, and for-profit companies with up to 3 employees; a paid Company Licence for for-profit organisations with more than three. The second split matters more if you are building a product rather than a video: Remotion for Creators — seat-based, intended for low-volume rendering within and for your own company, explicitly not for serving personalised videos to your end users. Remotion for Automators — render-based, which is the tier you land in the moment an agent renders videos for customers. From version 5.0 it carries mandatory telemetry reporting with a license key. So "my agent generates a video per signup" is not a Creators use case. Price it as Automators before you ship it. If that is a dealbreaker, Motion Canvas is MIT and covers a lot of the same ground.
documents.s: Remotion's licence is the gotcha, not the code

documents.t: This one burns people who have never heard of it, and it also explains an observation from the HN thread — that strong coding models write worse Manim than you would expect, with community reports that Gemini currently handles it better than Opus 5.5. There are two Manims: 3b1b/manim — Grant Sanderson's original, the one from the famous videos, ~94k stars, installed as manimgl. ManimCommunity/manim — the community fork, ~41k stars, the one that is actually documented and maintained for general use, installed as manim. They are API-incompatible and both are imported as from manim import *. Every tutorial, StackOverflow answer and blog post in the training corpus is one or the other, unlabelled. So the model writes plausible code that mixes both dialects, and Python raises on a method that exists in the other fork. It is not a reasoning failure; it is a poisoned-namespace failure. The fix is boring and it works: pin the fork in your prompt and in your environment, and give the agent the version's real API surface instead of letting it recall one. Pin the Manim dialect before the agent writes a line CopyOpen in Claude↗ Use ManimCommunity Manim (the "manim" package on PyPI), NOT 3b1b/manimgl. Before writing any scene, run: python -c "import manim; print(manim.__version__)" and confirm the version. If a class or method you want is not in that version's API, do not use it — check with: python -c "import manim; print([n for n in dir(manim) if 'Text' in n])" Never mix manimgl APIs (e.g. ShowCreation) with community APIs (Create).
documents.s: The Manim trap: two forks, one import name

documents.t: The same poisoned-corpus problem hits Remotion for a different reason: the library moved faster than the training data. In current Remotion, media components live in @remotion/media, and the trimming props are trimBefore / trimAfter. Preview and render can even use different components deliberately — Html5Audio from remotion while previewing, Audio from @remotion/media when rendering, switched on useRemotionEnvironment(). A model trained mostly on older material writes import {Audio} from 'remotion' with startFrom, which is the old shape. That code may still run. It may also silently do nothing useful, which is worse. This is exactly why Remotion publishes official Agent Skills — a set of twelve skills that hand an agent the current best practices instead of hoping it remembers them. They are designed for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and friends, and they follow the same open format covered in SKILL.md as an open standard. Install Remotion's official agent skills CopyOpen in Claude↗ npx skills add remotion-dev/skills The skills are granular, which is the point — you invoke the one that matches the phase of work: /remotion-create to scaffold, /remotion-markup for animation and typography, /remotion-studio to preview, /remotion-render to render, /remotion-captions for subtitles, plus remotion-best-practices as the umbrella when you are not sure. Vendor-maintained skills are the cheapest available fix for a model's stale knowledge of a fast-moving library: one install, and the agent stops guessing.

The single biggest quality lever is not a better prompt for the whole video. It is splitting the job so the model does judgement work and the renderer does determinism work — with a human-readable artefact in between. Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Generate a storyboard as data, not as code⌄ Ask for a JSON scene list first: per scene, a title, the on-screen text, the visual intent, and a duration in seconds. This is the cheap, reviewable step. You can read twelve scenes in thirty seconds and fix the narrative before a single component exists — and fixing the story is the edit that most improves the video. Code generated from a reviewed storyboard is also far more consistent than code generated from a paragraph of vibes. ←PreviousNext→ 2Fix the pacing in the storyboard, before any rendering⌄ Do the reading-speed arithmetic below on each scene's text and clamp the durations. Doing this at the data layer costs nothing; doing it after the components exist means re-timing every animation that depends on the scene length. ←PreviousNext→ 3Write the voiceover script per scene, then synthesise it⌄ Script per scene, not per video, so audio boundaries line up with visual boundaries. Synthesise each scene to its own audio file with a TTS API. Then measure the real duration of each clip — the synthesised audio is the ground truth for scene length, not your estimate. ←PreviousNext→ 4Re-derive scene durations from the real audio⌄ This is the step everyone skips and it is why so many AI explainers have visuals racing ahead of the narration. Read each audio file's actual duration, convert to frames, and feed those durations back into the composition as props. Never hardcode a frame count you guessed. ←PreviousNext→ 5Build the components from the storyboard, frame-derived only⌄ Now let the agent write the animation code, scene by scene, against the frozen storyboard. Enforce the determinism rule: every value from useCurrentFrame() and interpolate(), randomness from a seeded helper, no CSS transitions. Preview in the studio — a real preview catches layout errors that no amount of code reading does. ←PreviousNext→ 6Add captions from the audio you already have⌄ Do not ask the model to guess word timings. Transcribe your own voiceover locally and use the token-level timestamps. Remotion ships install-whisper-cpp for exactly this: installWhisperCpp(), downloadWhisperModel(), then transcribe() with token-level timestamps on, and toCaptions() to post-process. Captions are also the cheapest accessibility win available and they are what makes the video watchable muted. ←PreviousNext→ 7Render, then measure the render⌄ Render from the CLI so it is reproducible in CI. Then tune concurrency with a real measurement instead of a guess — Remotion has a benchmark command that runs the same render repeatedly across several concurrency values and compares them. ←PreviousNext→ Render from the CLI, then find your real concurrency CopyOpen in Claude↗ # deterministic render, reproducible in CI npx remotion render src/index.ts MyExplainer out/video.mp4 # stop guessing --concurrency: measure it npx remotion benchmark src/index.ts MyExplainer --concurrencies=2,4,8 --runs=3

The most consistent complaint in the HN thread was not that the videos looked bad. It was that they moved too fast to read. Slides appear, text animates in, and it is gone before a human finishes the sentence. This is a bug with a formula, not a matter of taste. Adult reading speed for unfamiliar screen text sits around 200–250 words per minute, and a viewer also needs time to find the new text before starting to read it. So: # minimum dwell time for a text block, in frames words = number of words in the block wpm = 200 # conservative for unfamiliar on-screen text settle = 0.4 # seconds to notice and locate the new text exit = 0.3 # seconds of breathing room before it leaves dwell_seconds = settle + (words / wpm) * 60 + exit dwell_frames = ceil(dwell_seconds * fps) # worked example: a 14-word bullet at 30 fps # 0.4 + (14 / 200) * 60 + 0.3 = 4.9 s -> 147 frames Two notes that make this actually useful: Animate in fast, hold long. The entrance transition should be 200–400 ms; the hold is where the dwell budget goes. Models tend to do the opposite — a long elegant fade, then a short hold. If narration exists, the dwell floor is the narration length. Text must stay up at least as long as the sentence describing it. Which is why deriving scene duration from the synthesised audio (step 4 above) fixes pacing almost for free. Clamp every scene to max(dwell_frames, narration_frames) and a large fraction of the "AI slop video" feeling disappears, with no change to the visuals at all.
documents.s: Pacing: the reason most AI explainers are unwatchable

documents.t: Community reports from the HN thread put a complete generated explainer at roughly $3–$4 in API spend, with the notable detail that the cost was dominated by image-model calls, not by the language model. One commenter reported generating a 5-minute video on an M4 MacBook Air in about 5 minutes of wall-clock time using an orchestrated pipeline. Treat the absolute numbers as perishable, but the shape is structural and worth planning around: The LLM is cheap here. A storyboard plus a few hundred lines of animation code is a small number of tokens. Even at flagship pricing it is cents. See what AI costs across providers. Per-asset generative calls dominate. Every generated image or b-roll clip is a separate paid call, and they multiply by scene count. This is the line item to cap. Compute is yours. Rendering runs on your machine or your CI, so it is time and electricity rather than API spend — until you move it to a serverless renderer, at which point it becomes both. Re-renders are nearly free, which is the whole structural advantage. Fixing a typo on slide 4 costs one render, not one regeneration. Localising into twelve languages costs twelve TTS runs and twelve renders, not twelve videos. The practical budgeting move: generate images once, commit them as assets, and keep re-renders asset-free. A pipeline that re-generates imagery on every render is the one that produces a surprising bill.
documents.s: What it costs, and which line item dominates

documents.t: The sharpest criticism in the thread is the one worth taking seriously: within weeks of these tools spreading, the outputs became recognisable. Same gradient backgrounds, same spring-in cards, same three-word bullets, same brisk voice. Several commenters also flagged repetitive copy and, in one case, a video confidently about the wrong subject entirely — a Twilight Imperium reference site described as an AI data startup. If you use this seriously, the levers that measurably de-generify output: Supply the design system, don't let it be invented. Pass your real palette, type scale, spacing scale and logo as constants the components import. Underspecified prompts are exactly where a model's house style leaks in. Write the copy yourself, or edit it hard. The visuals are the part models are good at. The narrative is the part that reads as generated. Use your own screen recordings as the hero asset. Real product footage composited into a generated scene is the single strongest anti-sameness move, and it also fixes the hallucination risk — the video cannot misdescribe your product if the product is on screen. Verify the claims like documentation. Anything factual in an explainer is a factual claim being published in your name, with none of a text page's easy correction path. Check it before you render, not after it is on YouTube. Break one convention on purpose. One deliberate choice that the default template would not make — an odd aspect ratio, silence where music is expected, a hand-drawn asset — is usually enough to stop the output reading as machine default.

Worth being honest, because the sceptics in that thread had a point: much of what gets produced is an animated slide deck with a voiceover. That is a perfectly good artefact for a changelog, a launch, a release note or an onboarding walkthrough — and a poor substitute for actual teaching, which needs a worked example, a wrong turn, and a reason to care. Reach for the code-driven pipeline when: The content must be exactly right — real UI, real numbers, real diagrams. You will need to change it later, or ship it in several languages. The same template will produce many videos from different data. Reach for something else when the goal is photographic footage (use a video model), or when the value is in a human explaining a hard idea badly and then well — which is still the thing no pipeline produces. Check yourself 0/5
documents.s: What this is good at, and what it isn't

documents.t: Opus 5.5 is good at explainer videos — Hacker News discussion — the thread this page is built around: 319 points, 175 comments, the reported workflows (HTML + JS timed animations captured with ffmpeg), the ~$3–$4 costs, the Manim weakness, the pacing complaints and the sameness criticism. Community reports, not vendor claims — treated as such throughout. Remotion — the React-based renderer. See useCurrentFrame() and interpolate() for the determinism model, random() for why Math.random() is banned and what the seeded PRNG returns, and the licence pages for the Company Licence, the Creators/Automators split and the v5.0 telemetry requirement. remotion-dev/skills — Remotion's twelve official Agent Skills for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others, installable with npx skills add remotion-dev/skills. The clearest current example of a vendor shipping agent-facing docs to fix stale model knowledge. @remotion/install-whisper-cpp — local transcription for captions: installWhisperCpp(), downloadWhisperModel(), transcribe() with token-level timestamps, and toCaptions() for post-processing. npx remotion benchmark — measures render time across concurrency values instead of guessing a flag. Motion Canvas — MIT, TypeScript, generator-based timelines. The licence-free alternative when Remotion's Company Licence is a blocker. ManimCommunity/manim and 3b1b/manim — both MIT, both imported as manim, mutually incompatible. The root cause of the Manim failure mode above.
